docs.title: Getting Started in C
docs.text: This lab will be getting used to Code::Blocks, and trying different additions to familiarise yourself with the environment and the syntax.

docs.title: printf()
docs.text:
As you have noticed, the initial startup of Code::Blocks has a code template that looks like:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

int main()
{
    printf("Hello world!\n");
    return 0;
}

Which shows the baseline structure of a C program. The first 2 lines, which start with #include, are known as the libraries of C. These are a collection of programs and commands that allow us to quickly integrate them into our program. for example, the library stdio.h (standard input output), contains the function printf that is used in the default code.

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
Comments are an important documentation method to ensure your code is interpretable to other people. Any words after // are ignored by your program.

// A comment
printf("Hello World\n"); // A comment after some code

docs.title: Inputs and Outputs
docs.text:
With C it is straight forward to input information, as well as output information as we have seen. For this code we have declared an integer withint n;, which is an empty variable that the code can now change.

#include <stdio.h>

int main()
{
    int n; //declare an integer

    printf("Please enter a number: "); // Prompt the user
    scanf("%d", &n); // reading an integer input
    printf("You entered: %d\n", n); // printing an integer output
    return 0;
}

Run this code and see what happens. The terminal will wait for a user input before printing it out again. The syntax for %d and &n will be covered in a later lab, but just know %d is to let the program know it is looking for an integer, and &n is to inform the program where to save the entered value.

docs.title: Variables, Data Types, Libraries, Inputs and Output in C
Variables and Data Types
docs.text:
Variables refers to the data that will be used by the code in various means. C needs explicitly informing what data type it is storing in each variable, to ensure it can carry out the correct calculations.

Data Type Description Example Size int Signed integer (whole numbers) int radius = 6; 16 or 32 bits char Single ASCII character or 8-bit integer char status = 'A'; 8 bits (1 byte) float Single-precision floating-point number float voltage = 3.3f; 32 bits (4 bytes)

docs.title: Declaring Variables
docs.text:
Similar to the previous lab, where we declared int, we can declare other variables in the same way

#include <stdio.h>

int main()
{
    int age;
    float temperature = 21.5;
    char grade = 'A';

    int age = 25;
    return 0;
}

As shown with int, you can declare any variable and assign a value later.

docs.title: Output Variables
docs.text:
In C, to output a variable, we will need to use format specifiers. each variable has its own format specifiers.

Data Type Format Specifier int %d char %c float %f

An example of using a format specifier for a float is shown below:


int main()
{
    float temperature = 21.5;
    printf("Temperature: %f\n", temperature);
    printf("Temperature: %.2f\n", temperature); // two decimal places
    return 0;
}

docs.title: Basic Operators
docs.text:
Operators allow the program to change the variables given, such as arithmetic and character alteration.

Below is the standard operators

int a = 10;
int b = 3;

printf("Addition: %d\n", a + b);
printf("Subtraction: %d\n", a - b);
printf("Multiplication: %d\n", a * b);
printf("Division: %d\n", a / b);

docs.text:

docs.title: Deep Dive: What #include <stdio.h> Actually Does
docs.text:
At the start of the lab, we glossed over #include <stdio.h> as "the header file needed for printf()". Here is what is happening under the hood:

  1. Pre-processor Pass: Before compilation begins, the C preprocessor (cpp) literally copy-pastes the entire contents of stdio.h into the top of your source file.
  2. Function Prototypes: It tells the compiler the exact memory signature of printf() so it knows how many arguments and byte widths to expect on the call stack.
  3. Register/Peripheral Mapping: In embedded C, header files perform this same trick to define hardware register addresses (e.g., #define GPIOA_BASE (0x40020000UL)).

docs.title: Installing Code::Blocks
docs.text:
Managed DesktopPersonal Computer

Code::Blocks is available on the managed PC software library; IDE and MinGW (GCC compiler for Windows) installed. In the Computer lab for the module, the software will be installed, in other locations you need to use the “Software Center” (icon on desktop) and search for the program to install.

• Go to http://www.codeblocks.org/downloads

• Click on ‘Download the binary release’

• Scroll to the ‘Microsoft Windows' section

• Select codeblocks-xx.xxmingw-setup.exe and click on Sourceforge.net (this should automatically start the download). NOTE: xx.xx is just whatever the current version number is.

• Click ‘Run’ (at the bottom of the screen)

• Install the Codeblocks application using the install wizard (you might need to minimise the web browser)

• After you have finished installing, click ‘Yes’ for Do you want to run Codeblocks now?

• Click ‘GNU GCC Compiler, then click ‘OK’

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
Step 1Step 2Step 3Step 4Step 5Step 6Step 7

Open Code::Blocks on your computer, and select "Create a new project" (or existing)

Select console application

In the wizard setup, ensure you select cm and continue

The compiler should be set up automatically like this, but double check

On the left side of your screen, right click the project, and select "Build options..."

Scroll down to warnings, and ensure "Enable all common compiler warnings (overrides many other settings)" is enabled. click OK

Flags determine how the compiler behaves, these are set though the IDE GUI (you’ll see this in a ‘make’ file later in course ).

Open main.c, and click "Build and Run" shown. this should compile your code and run it in a terminal.

docs.title: Compiler settings
docs.text: In "Settings" -> "Compiler", make sure the the compiler follows the [-std=c99] standard. This will be important to ensure your code runs the same as everyone elses.

docs.title: Debugging and Error Messages
docs.text:
Debugging is the process of removing errors from the code written. Errors can be compiling issues, ie big red text, or mistakes in the code due to the operator (you).

Luckily, Code::Blocks has multiple techniques to bugfix:

docs.title: Setting Up Your Project for Debugging
docs.text:
Before you can debug, you must have a project. If you're working with a single C file, create a new "Console application" project and add your file to it.

• Go to File > New > Project...

• Select Console application, and click Go.

• Choose C as the language.

• Give your project a name and save it.

• Add your C source file to the project.

docs.title: Setting Breakpoints
docs.text:
A breakpoint is a marker you place on a line of code where you want the program execution to pause. This allows you to inspect the program's state at that specific point.

• Open your C source file in the editor.

• Click in the gray margin to the left of the line number where you want to set a breakpoint. A red circle will appear, indicating the breakpoint is active.

docs.title: Starting the Debugger
docs.text:
Once you have your breakpoints set, you can start the debugging session.

• Go to Debug > Start/Continue.

• Alternatively, you can press the F9 key.

The program will run until it hits the first breakpoint, and the line will be highlighted.

docs.title: Stepping Through Code
docs.text:
While the program is paused at a breakpoint, you can use these commands to control its execution:

• F7 (Next line): Executes the current line of code and moves to the next one. This is the most common command for stepping through your program.

• F8 (Next instruction): Similar to F7 but is more detailed, sometimes stepping into assembly instructions. Use F7 for most cases.

• F4 (Next line of code - skip functions): Skips over function calls, executing the entire function and stopping on the line after it returns. Use this to avoid stepping through functions you know are correct.

docs.title: Watching Variables
docs.text:
One of the most powerful features of a debugger is the ability to inspect the values of variables in real-time.

• Go to Debug > Debugging Windows > Watches.

• In the "Watches" window that appears, you can see the values of variables as you step through the code.

• You can add a variable to the watch list by right-clicking it in the editor and selecting "Add watch" or by manually typing its name in the "Watches" window.

docs.title: Common C Error Messages and How to Interpret Them
docs.text:
expected ';' before 'token'

Meaning: The compiler expects a semicolon at a certain point but found something else instead.

Common Causes:

  • Forgetting a semicolon at the end of a statement.
  • This error can sometimes appear on the line after the actual error, as the compiler doesn't realize the semicolon is missing until it sees the next line of code.
conflicting types for 'variable_name'

Meaning: You have declared the same variable or function with two different data types.

Common Causes:

  • Declaring a global variable with one type and then a local variable in a function with the same name and a different type.
  • Declaring a function prototype with one return type but defining the function with another.
'variable_name' undeclared (first use in this function)

Meaning: The compiler has no record of the variable you are trying to use.

Common Causes:

  • Forgetting to declare the variable before using it.
  • Misspelling the variable name. C is case-sensitive, so myVar and myvar are treated as different variables.
warning: format '%d' expects type 'int *', but argument '2' has type 'int'

Meaning: You are using the wrong format specifier in a function like scanf or printf. This specific message means you passed an int instead of a pointer to an int to scanf.

Common Causes:

  • Using scanf("%d", num); instead of the correct scanf("%d", &num);. The & operator passes the variable address so scanf can store the value.
  • Using the wrong format specifier, e.g., %f for a double instead of %lf.
undefined reference to 'function_name'

Meaning: The linker cannot find the implementation/definition for a function that you called.

Common Causes:

  • Forgetting to include a library header file (e.g., <string.h> for strlen()).
  • Misspelling the function name in the code or header.
  • Trying to use a function from an external library that has not been properly linked during compilation.
